Mr. John S. Barratt belonged to a family of cultured and prominent people in Fannin County. A brother, T. E. Barratt, was a minister of the Christian Church and editor of the Christian Messenger. Dr. Lassiter, the footsteps of a former teacher at Savoy, recalls that in 1875 or 1876, Mr. S. Barratt taught school at Lamius, near Dodd City, in Fannin County, and that his school-house was destroyed by a storm. From 1878 until the cyclone of 1880 he taught in Savoy. His home there was wrecked just a week before the cyclone, and with his family he was domiciled in the section house of the railroad company when the storm struck; left Savoy to accept the principalship of the Oak Cliff high school in Dallas. He died in Dallas about 1898, leaving three sons, J. J. and Foster Barratt, now in Dallas, and W. T. Barratt, who is now a druggist now in Sherman, in 1938.

Miss Tennie Deatherage, the daughter of John E. and Hannah (Campbell) Deatherage, was raised in the neighborhood of Savoy and was probably a student in the College before her teaching. She married a successful farmer, William J. Hood, the husband of her deceased sister, Mary, and helped him to farm a large acreage in this area.

Miss Emma Lacy was likewise a member of a well-known Savoy family, as she was the daughter of R. W. Lacy and his wife, Nancy (Thompson) Lacy. Both of both families had been in the area since before the War. She was a teacher in the preparatory department from approximately 1882-1884, according to the recollection of her sister, Mrs. Y. E. Conner. She married George E. Standifer some ten years after her work in Savoy, and died in Whitewright, Texas, in 1920.
